title: PAUL TOLD HUSBANDS AND WIVES NOT TO SEXUALLY DEPRIVE EACH OTHER—BUT THAT VERSE HAS BEEN ABUSED
paragraphs: PAUL TOLD HUSBANDS AND WIVES NOT TO SEXUALLY DEPRIVE EACH OTHER—BUT THAT VERSE HAS BEEN ABUSED

1 Corinthians 7 was never permission to demand someone’s body in the name of God. Read Paul’s actual words carefully, and something far more beautiful—and far more challenging—emerges: mutual belonging, mutual responsibility, mutual tenderness, and a marriage transformed by the self-giving love of Christ.
There is a sentence from the Bible that has followed some husbands and wives into their bedrooms like a threat.
“Do not deprive one another.”

For some married couples, those words have been life-giving. They have reminded two tired, distracted people that intimacy matters. That marriage should not slowly become two roommates sharing bills, children, responsibilities, and a surname while their hearts live miles apart.
But for others, those same words have been weaponized.
“You cannot tell me no.”
“The Bible says your body belongs to me.”
“You are sinning if you refuse.”
“You owe me.”

And somewhere in a bedroom where Scripture should have brought light, a husband or wife has lain awake wondering whether God Himself was demanding something from them that felt frightening, humiliating, painful, coercive, or emotionally devastating.
But what if Paul never said what they were told he said?
What if we have sometimes taken a passage about mutual marital self-giving and twisted it into unilateral entitlement?
Because when you actually slow down and read 1 Corinthians 7, something remarkable happens.
Paul destroys the very argument used by someone who wants to turn this passage into a weapon.
He does it with one word repeated through the passage:
Likewise.

Paul is answering questions from believers in Corinth concerning marriage, sexuality, singleness, and abstinence. He begins the chapter by referring to matters about which the Corinthians had written to him. The surrounding discussion shows that sexual abstinence itself was part of the controversy. Paul responds by affirming marriage and mutual marital responsibility.
Then comes the passage so often quoted:
“The husband should give to his wife her conjugal rights, and likewise the wife to her husband.”
Then Paul says something extraordinarily countercultural:
“For the wife does not have authority over her own body, but the husband does.”
Someone determined to dominate could stop reading right there.
And tragically, some people effectively have.
But Paul does not stop.
“Likewise the husband does not have authority over his own body, but the wife does.”
That second sentence changes everything.
The Greek makes the symmetry unmistakable:
“ἡ γυνὴ τοῦ ἰδίου σώματος οὐκ ἐξουσιάζει ἀλλὰ ὁ ἀνήρ· ὁμοίως δὲ καὶ ὁ ἀνὴρ τοῦ ἰδίου σώματος οὐκ ἐξουσιάζει ἀλλὰ ἡ γυνή.”
The crucial word is ὁμοίως — homoiōs.
Likewise.
In the same way.
Paul does not tell the wife that her body exists for her husband's desires while allowing the husband to remain sovereign over himself.
He places them both beneath the same radical principle.
Her body is not something she uses selfishly against him.
His body is not something he uses selfishly against her.
Marriage is not one person possessing another.
It is two people learning covenantal self-giving.
That distinction matters enormously.
Because there is a universe of difference between saying, “Because I love you, I give myself to you,” and hearing, “Because you married me, I can take what I want from you.”
One sounds like covenant.
The other sounds like ownership.
And Jesus did not teach His people to love by domination.
Christian love reaches its highest definition at a cross.
Christ gives Himself.
He does not exploit.
He does not manipulate.
He does not use another person's vulnerability for selfish gratification.
The pattern of Christlike love is sacrificial: “Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her.” That is the atmosphere Christian marriage is meant to breathe.
Then Paul continues:
“Do not deprive one another, except perhaps by agreement for a limited time, that you may devote yourselves to prayer; but then come together again…”
Now look carefully at the Greek behind “by agreement”:
ἐκ συμφώνου — ek symphōnou.
It carries the idea of agreement together—mutual consent.
The word is related to the idea from which English gets “symphony”: voices sounding together.
Not one voice overpowering another.
Together.
Paul therefore does not picture one spouse announcing, “We are abstaining whether you like it or not.”
Nor does he picture another spouse saying, “You must give me sex whenever I demand it because verse 5 says not to deprive me.”
The temporary abstinence Paul describes is ἐκ συμφώνου—mutually agreed upon—and πρὸς καιρόν, for a limited time.
Even abstinence is treated relationally.
Even here, Paul sees two people who should talk, listen, care, agree, and eventually return to one another.
That means this passage confronts more than one kind of selfishness.
It confronts the spouse who deliberately weaponizes sex.
And it confronts the spouse who weaponizes Scripture to obtain sex.
Both can turn intimacy into power.
One says, “I will withhold myself until you suffer.”
The other says, “I will quote God until you surrender.”
Neither sounds like Jesus.
Sexual intimacy within marriage is not meant to become currency.
Not payment for good behavior.
Not punishment for bad behavior.
Not leverage.
Not revenge.
Not proof of masculinity.
Not proof of femininity.
Not a bargaining chip.
Not something extracted through guilt.
It is meant to belong within covenant love.
And that is precisely why this conversation requires tenderness.
Because behind the word “deprivation” there may be stories nobody sees.
Maybe she is not trying to punish him.
Maybe she is exhausted.
Maybe pregnancy changed her body.
Maybe childbirth left pain nobody prepared her for.
Maybe she spends all day being touched by children and reaches nighttime with nothing emotionally left.
Maybe she feels invisible everywhere except when someone wants something from her body.
Maybe he is not rejecting her.
Maybe he is ashamed.
Maybe stress has crushed his desire.
Maybe medication, illness, hormones, grief, depression, age, sexual dysfunction, relational wounds, or unresolved conflict have entered a marriage neither spouse expected.
Maybe there is betrayal that has never actually healed.
Maybe pornography shattered trust.
Maybe harsh words outside the bedroom made tenderness inside the bedroom feel impossible.
Maybe one spouse carries trauma from long before the wedding.
Maybe sex physically hurts.
Maybe somebody learned to smile while quietly dissociating.
And maybe the sentence “The Bible says you can't deprive me” did not heal any of it.
It only made the wound deeper.
Scripture should never be used to silence suffering that love should be willing to hear.
At the same time, another painful truth must also be spoken.
Sometimes intimacy really is withheld deliberately.
Sometimes affection becomes punishment.
Sometimes sex becomes a reward system.
Sometimes one spouse knows the other is lonely and uses that loneliness as leverage.
Sometimes months become years, communication dies, resentment grows, and nobody wants to say what is happening.
Paul's words confront that too.
Biblical correction cuts in both directions.
The spouse who says, “Your needs never matter to me,” should hear Paul's call to mutual care.
The spouse who says, “Your boundaries never matter to me,” should hear it too.
Marriage does not give Christians permission to become selfish in opposite directions.
It calls them into something harder.
Love.
Patient love.
Truthful love.
Listening love.
Repentant love.
Love that asks instead of assumes.
Love that notices tears.
Love that cares whether the other person feels safe.
Love that refuses to punish.
Love that refuses to manipulate.
Love willing to say, “Something between us is hurting. Can we talk about it?”
And sometimes love says, “We need help.”

There is no shame in a married couple seeking wise pastoral counsel, qualified marriage counseling, or appropriate medical care when pain, trauma, dysfunction, medication effects, hormonal changes, disability, illness, or deep relational wounds are affecting intimacy.
Prayer matters.
Scripture matters.
And getting appropriate help does not compete with faithfulness to God.
Sometimes seeking help is one of the ways we stop hiding.
But there is something even deeper in Paul's language that modern readers can easily miss.
In a world where sexual double standards were hardly unusual, Paul deliberately gives husband and wife corresponding responsibilities.
“The husband…”
“Likewise the wife…”
“The wife…”
“Likewise the husband…”
“Do not deprive one another…”
This is reciprocity.
Not entitlement.
The bedroom becomes one more place where the Christian learns the death of selfishness.
And suddenly the passage becomes much more uncomfortable than the weaponized version.
Because the weaponized version lets me ask:
“What am I owed?”
The Gospel-shaped version makes me ask:
“How am I loving?”
That question reaches farther than sex.
Have I become emotionally unavailable?
Have I stopped being affectionate except when I want intercourse?
Have I treated my spouse like a sexual vending machine—attention inserted, sex expected?
Have I rejected my spouse repeatedly without caring enough to explain what is happening?
Have I used spiritual language to avoid an honest conversation?
Have I made my spouse afraid to tell me no?
Have I punished vulnerability?
Have I ignored pain?
Have I allowed resentment to become a wall and then pretended the wall appeared by itself?
Have I demanded tenderness while refusing to be tender?
And perhaps the hardest question:
Have I ever used God's Word to win against the person I vowed to love?
That question should make every Christian tremble.
Because the Bible was never given to us as ammunition for controlling other people.
The Word exposes us too.
Before you quote 1 Corinthians 7:5 at your husband or wife, stand beneath it yourself.
Before asking what your spouse owes you, ask what Christ is changing in you.
Your selfishness.
Your pride.
Your resentment.
Your lust.
Your coldness.
Your impatience.
Your manipulation.
Your refusal to communicate.
Your unwillingness to forgive.
Your unwillingness to repent.
This is where the scandal meets grace.
Because perhaps you have failed here.
Maybe badly.
Maybe you pressured someone you claimed to love.
Maybe you withheld affection to hurt them.
Maybe you mocked your spouse's body.
Maybe pornography taught your mind to consume instead of cherish.
Maybe rejection became bitterness.
Maybe bitterness became cruelty.
Maybe years of silence now sit between you in bed.
Maybe you are reading this and realizing that something you called “biblical authority” was actually selfishness wearing a Bible verse.
What now?
Jesus.
Not hiding.
Not pretending.
Jesus.
The Gospel does not tell sinners to manufacture innocence.
It tells sinners where forgiveness can be found.
Christ went to the cross for real sin.
Sexual sin.
Marital sin.
Secret sin.
Religious hypocrisy.
Manipulation.
Lust.
Pride.
Cruelty.
Bitterness.
All the ugly things we would rather rename than confess.
At Calvary, Jesus did not die for the imaginary version of you that never wounded anyone.
He died for sinners.
And repentance means we stop defending what He is calling us to surrender.
Sometimes repentance sounds like this:
“I was wrong.”
No excuse afterward.
No “but you…”
Just truth.
“I pressured you.”
“I ignored your pain.”
“I punished you with rejection.”
“I used Scripture against you.”
“I stopped listening.”
“I let pornography corrupt the way I looked at you.”
“I made intimacy about myself.”
“I need forgiveness.”
That may not instantly repair everything.
Forgiveness does not magically erase consequences, restore trust overnight, or eliminate the need for safety, counsel, accountability, medical treatment, or patient rebuilding.
But repentance opens the door that pride keeps locked.
And grace walks through doors like that.
This is what Jesus does.
He enters places shame told us to hide.
He exposes what darkness told us to protect.
Then He does something scandalous.
He offers mercy.
Not cheap mercy that calls evil good.
Grace tells the truth about sin and then announces that sin does not have to write the final chapter.
The cross proves both things simultaneously.
Sin is serious enough that Christ died.
Grace is powerful enough that Christ rose.
So perhaps your marriage does not need another argument over who owes whom sex.
Perhaps it needs two people kneeling before Jesus again.
Perhaps it needs confession.
Perhaps it needs forgiveness.
Perhaps it needs a difficult conversation.
Perhaps it needs months of rebuilding trust.
Perhaps it needs professional help.
Perhaps it needs tenderness without expectation.
Perhaps it needs intimacy rediscovered slowly, patiently, prayerfully.
Perhaps it needs husband and wife looking at each other not as competitors keeping score, but as two redeemed sinners learning how to love because Christ first loved them.
Paul was not handing husbands a weapon.
He was not handing wives one either.
He was calling married Christians away from selfish isolation and toward mutuality.
And if somebody ever quotes, “Do not deprive one another,” while conveniently forgetting ἐκ συμφώνου, mutual agreement, and ὁμοίως, likewise, read the whole passage.
Context matters.
Words matter.
Your spouse matters.
And Christ matters most.
If this exposed something you have hidden even from yourself, you do not need to tell strangers every detail of your marriage. But you can take one honest step into the light.
No explanations required.
Someone reading those words may realize tonight that they are not the only Christian struggling behind a smiling family photograph.

Someone in your circle may have spent years believing that God endorsed the very coercion that wounded them. Someone else may need to realize that deliberately weaponizing rejection is not loving either.
And whether you ever spend a cent or not, keep pursuing Christ.
Because your marriage was never meant to become a courtroom where two people argue over their rights.
At its most Christlike, it becomes a place where two redeemed people keep learning how to give, listen, repent, forgive, protect, cherish, and love.
And maybe that is the sentence somebody needs tonight:
Jesus can enter even the room where love became a weapon—and teach wounded hearts how to become tender again.
